t: What the core Flight System Is
title: What the core Flight System Is
description: NASA's core Flight System (cFS) is a reusable, platform-independent flight software framework built by NASA Goddard Space Flight Center. It separates portable core services from mission applications so the same flight software can fly on many spacecraft with only a thin platform layer changed. The project is open source and has flown on real missions including GPM, MMS, LADEE, and DART.

facts.Architecture: cFE core + OSAL + PSP + mission apps

provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: cFE Executive Services (ES)
description: Executive Services is the cFE core service that manages the lifecycle of flight applications: creation, deletion, restart, and system startup sequencing. ES also owns the system log, the exception and reset handling, and the software bus memory pools that applications allocate from. Every cFS application registers with ES before it can send or receive a single message.

facts.Duties: app lifecycle, startup, system log, resets

provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: The cFS Software Bus (SB)
description: The Software Bus is the publish/subscribe message backbone of cFS: applications never call each other directly, they publish CCSDS packets addressed by message ID and subscribe to the IDs they need. This decoupling lets teams develop and test apps independently and rewire data flows by configuration instead of code changes. SB enforces pipe depth limits and routes packets in priority order.

facts.Benefit: apps decoupled, data flow by config

provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Event Services (EVS) and Flight Telemetry
description: Event Services gives every application a uniform way to report what it is doing: apps send event messages with a severity from debug to critical, and EVS filters, counts, and forwards them to telemetry. Operators on the ground see one consistent event stream instead of a dozen app-specific log formats. EVS also supports binary event filters so noisy events can be throttled without rebuilding the app.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Table Services (TBL) — Uploadable Configuration
description: Table Services lets operators upload new configuration to a running spacecraft without rebuilding flight software: parameters live in tables that can be validated, activated, and dumped. A table has an inactive buffer for ground edits and an active buffer the app actually uses, with CRC validation on load. This is how gains, limits, and schedules get tuned after launch.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Time Services (TIME) — Spacecraft Clock
description: Time Services maintains the spacecraft clock: mission elapsed time, conversion between MET and UTC, and 1 Hz timing signals that drive the scheduler. TIME handles leap seconds and clock correlation so telemetry timestamps line up with ground UTC. Deterministic time is what makes scheduled commanding and science data tagging possible.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: OSAL — Operating System Abstraction Layer
description: The Operating System Abstraction Layer is what makes cFS platform-independent: it presents one POSIX-like API for tasks, queues, semaphores, timers, and file I/O, with implementations for RTEMS, VxWorks, and Linux underneath. Mission code calls OSAL and never touches the RTOS directly. Porting cFS to a new board mostly means implementing the small PSP layer, not rewriting applications.

facts.Rule: apps never touch the RTOS directly

provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: PSP — Platform Support Package
description: The Platform Support Package is the thin board-specific layer under OSAL: it owns boot code, the system timer tick, UART/SpaceWire drivers, EEPROM access, and watchdog handling. Each processor board gets its own PSP while everything above stays identical. A new mission computer joins the cFS family by writing a PSP, typically a few thousand lines.

facts.Effect: one PSP per board, apps portable

provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

t: Sample Applications: SCH, HK, and Friends
title: Sample Applications: SCH, HK, and Friends
description: cFS ships with sample applications that form a working starter flight software load: SCH (scheduler) sends timed messages, HK (housekeeping) gathers telemetry, and others cover stored commands, memory peek/poke, and file management. New missions clone these samples as templates for their own apps. The samples are also the standard cFS training path.

facts.Others: stored commands, mem utils, file mgr

provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

t: CCSDS Space Packets on the Bus
title: CCSDS Space Packets on the Bus
description: Every cFS software-bus message is a CCSDS Space Packet: a 6-byte primary header with version, type, secondary-header flag, APID, sequence flags/count, and packet length, followed by the data. The APID (application process ID) is the address — the message ID on the bus maps directly to it. Ground systems speak the same packets, so flight-to-ground is seamless.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Building cFS with CMake
description: Modern cFS builds with CMake: a top-level build config selects the PSP, OSAL BSP, and the set of mission applications, then compiles everything into one flight image. Sample targets build for Linux (for desktop testing), RTEMS, and VxWorks from the same source tree. Continuous integration builds all targets on every commit.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: Missions That Fly cFS
description: cFS has flown on a growing list of real NASA missions: the Global Precipitation Measurement (GPM) mission, the Magnetospheric Multiscale (MMS) mission, LADEE at the Moon, and DART, which flew cFS-derived software to its asteroid impact. Each mission reused the same core and wrote only mission-specific applications. That reuse is the entire economic argument for cFS.

t: Testing cFS: Coverage and Functional Tests
title: Testing cFS: Coverage and Functional Tests
description: cFS is tested like flight software must be: unit tests with coverage requirements on the core services, functional tests that run the whole stack on Linux, and static analysis on every change. The open-source repository runs these checks in CI so a broken commit cannot merge quietly. Coverage reports track which lines of cFE/OSAL/PSP the tests actually execute.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

t: cFS on RTOS vs Linux: The Portability Proof
title: cFS on RTOS vs Linux: The Portability Proof
description: The portability proof of cFS is that the same application source runs on Linux for development and on RTEMS or VxWorks for flight, with only the PSP and OSAL implementation swapped. Developers debug on a laptop, then the identical code flies. Timing behavior differs — Linux is not real-time — so final verification always happens on the flight-like target.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.

title: End-to-End: Command In, Telemetry Out
description: The full cFS loop in one picture: a ground command arrives as a CCSDS packet, the software bus routes it to the right app, the app acts and publishes housekeeping, EVS logs the event, and HK gathers it into the downlink telemetry frame. Tables let the ground retune behavior without new software. Fifteen records up the ladder, this is the whole machine working as one.
provenance: Public record: compiled from official project documentation and published specifications. Fact-checked 2026-10-21.
